issue.title: Early secondary school: GCSE courses or a broader curriculum?
issue.question: Should the first three years of secondary school be for GCSE preparation, or for something wider, and who decides?
issue.summary: On 8 November 2026 the Department for Education said Key Stage 3 will be restored as a distinct three-year phase of the National Curriculum, with schools told not to start GCSE courses early for large groups or routinely narrow options earlier (s1). The department says persistent absence almost doubles between Years 7 and 9, rising to one in four children, and that some schools start GCSE teaching as early as Year 7 (s1). A survey of 810 teachers in England, commissioned by the International Baccalaureate, found 57% named GCSE preparation as a leading influence on Key Stage 3 (s2). The full new National Curriculum is due later in 2026 (s1).
issue.slot_reason: Schools had not come up yet in the simulation, and the government's plan for the first years of secondary school was in the UK news that day.

news.headline: Government restores Key Stage 3 as a distinct phase in curriculum overhaul

poll.sample: 810 teachers and teaching assistants in England; 2,090 pupils aged 11 to 18; 743 parents with Key Stage 3 experience
poll.finding: 57% of teachers said GCSE preparation is a leading influence on Key Stage 3. Among teachers, 57% would keep GCSE preparation central and give Key Stage 3 a clearer identity, 26% would put more weight on skills, character and wider development, and 14% want a distinct curriculum with aims separate from GCSE preparation. Parents: about a quarter said GCSE preparation is now the main purpose of these years, but 11% said it should be the priority. The page gives 56% in one place and 57% in another for the keep-GCSE-central option, and does not show exact question wording. The study was commissioned by the International Baccalaureate.

bench.title: Turn the Key Stage 3 rule into an inspected, funded promise
bench.answer: The Department for Education has told schools not to start GCSE courses early for large groups or routinely narrow options, but gives no cost, start date or check (s1). Change it: the department would add a ring-fenced grant, so no school pays by cutting subjects or staff. School leaders warn that new duties without investment risk diluting what schools already offer (s3). The school inspectorate would then check, in every secondary inspection, how many pupils start GCSEs before Year 10 and whether options narrowed. Each school would publish its Year 7 to 9 timetable and absence rate in plain words. It worked if early starts fall and Year 7 to 9 persistent absence, one in four by Year 9 (s1), stops rising.

bench.title: Let each school's local panel decide what Years 7 to 9 are for
bench.answer: Instead of the Department for Education setting one rule from the centre (s1), each secondary school's governing body would add a panel drawn by lot from its teachers, parents and Year 7 to 9 pupils. The panel would sign off a published three-year plan, including whether any GCSE teaching starts early. That moves the choice away from exam pressure, which 57% of surveyed teachers named a leading influence (s2). The department would fund the panels' time, as school leaders warn extra duties without investment risk diluting provision (s3). It worked if absence, which the department says reaches one in four children by Year 9 (s1), falls, and more than 36% of pupils see learning's link beyond exams (s2).

bench.title: Three broad years, steered by families and teachers
bench.answer: In this simulation, Years 7 to 9 would offer broad learning, following the department’s call to stop routine early GCSE courses (s1). Each school would elect a council of pupils, parents and teachers to agree its teaching plan. Families would hold most seats; businesses could advise but buy no votes. The plan must protect reading, maths, science, arts, staff and existing support. Schools would publish a plain yearly account of lessons, spending and results. After three years, success would mean better attendance, fewer children behind in reading and maths, subjects retained, and more pupils able to show useful work beyond exam practice. Later GCSE results would check that standards held.

gate.verdict: Two of three pass the limits plainly (A on money, C on subjects and standards); none shows it would cut absence, because no source tests that. Facts cannot settle who should decide what Years 7 to 9 are for.

jury.question: Who should decide what Years 7 to 9 are for: the government, the inspectors, or each school's own families and teachers?
options: Government keeps the rule, with inspection and a funded grant
Each school's families and teachers decide, in the open
Elected school councils with a family majority, plus a national floor
Leave schools alone and let parents choose between them
jury.ruling: Each school's families and teachers decide, in the open. Five of the twelve jurors wanted the choice made by the people in the building, with plans and results published.

reasons.text: I studied late and wish someone had asked what the early years were for. Let the school say, in the open.
Keep the rule. In my day the exam board set it and it held. Add the money so nobody loses subjects.
Councils and panels are more committees. Parents should pick a school and leave when it lets them down.
Families should have the majority, but a national floor stops some schools doing nothing at all.

minister.trial: In 10 secondary schools that now start GCSE courses before Year 10, a panel of teachers, parents and Year 7 to 9 pupils, drawn by lot, signs off a published three-year plan for Years 7 to 9. The department funds the panel's time. Plans, timetables and absence rates are public.
minister.fail_number: Persistent absence in Years 7 to 9 in the 10 schools rising above their own 2026 rate (target: lower), or any school dropping a subject or cutting staff to fund the plan (target: none).
minister.statement: Quick quiz. Who knows best what Years 7 to 9 are for: the exam board, the department, or the people in the building? The jury leaned to the building. Five of twelve, not a landslide. So I'm signing one small thing. Ten schools, a panel drawn by lot, a plan on the school's own door. The department pays for the time, so nobody robs music to do it. The trade-off: some panels may pick the exam treadmill anyway. If they do, they have to say why, out loud.
